body:
Key Takeaways
  • Skyroot's Vikram-1 is India's first private rocket to reach orbit, achieving a 450-km Low Earth Orbit.
  • The launch, named 'Mission Aagaman,' took place on July 18, 2026, from Sriharikota.
  • Skyroot Aerospace, founded by ex-ISRO engineers, became India's first spacetech unicorn with a $1.1 billion valuation.
  • Prime Minister Modi hailed the launch as a defining moment for India's space journey and innovation.
India's Private Space Milestone
›First private Indian rocket to reach orbit.
›Achieved a 450-km Low Earth Orbit.
›Third country globally with private orbital capability.
›Launch occurred on July 18, 2026.
Skyroot Aerospace
  • Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 successfully reached a 450-km Low Earth Orbit on its maiden flight, making India the third country — after the United States and China — where a private company has achieved orbital launch capability.
  • The mission, dubbed 'Mission Aagaman,' lifted off from Sriharikota on July 18 after a brief planned hold, deploying multiple technology-demonstration payloads from domestic and international customers.
  • Founded by former ISRO engineers, Skyroot became India's first spacetech unicorn in May with a $1.1 billion valuation, and plans up to two more Vikram-1 launches this year.
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi called the launch "a defining moment in India's space journey" and personally congratulated the Skyroot team over phone.

On a Saturday afternoon that will be remembered as a turning point for India's space ambitions, a seven-storey-tall rocket built by a Hyderabad startup soared into the sky from Sriharikota and punched through to orbit — making Skyroot Aerospace the first private Indian company to accomplish a feat that until now only government agencies had achieved on Indian soil.

The Vikram-1 rocket, flying under the banner of 'Mission Aagaman' — meaning 'the arrival' — lifted off from the First Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at 12:05 PM IST on July 18, 2026. The launch had been briefly delayed from its original 11:30 AM schedule after the navigation team initiated a planned hold, but when the countdown resumed, the all-carbon-composite rocket rose cleanly on a column of fire, its four stages igniting in sequence as it climbed toward a 450-kilometer Low Earth Orbit.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2078378012186173749

"Mission Aagaman is a grand success," Skyroot announced. "This is a test flight. We will be doing a few of these before we move into routine commercial flights."

With this launch, India officially became the third nation in the world — after the United States and China — to have a fully private company design, build, and successfully send a rocket into orbit.

The Rocket: Seven Stories of Innovation

Standing 22 meters tall, Vikram-1 is a four-stage launch vehicle designed to carry payloads of up to 350 kg into Low Earth Orbit, or 290 kg into a Sun-Synchronous Orbit. The rocket's architecture combines three solid-fuel propulsion stages — named Kalam-1200, Kalam-250, and Kalam-100 after India's missile man — with a liquid-propellant fourth stage powered by a cluster of four Raman engines, each producing 3.4 kilonewtons of thrust.

What makes Vikram-1 technologically distinctive is its extensive use of advanced manufacturing. The rocket's structure is built entirely from carbon-composite materials, and several engine components are 3D-printed, reducing weight by 50% and cutting production time by 80%, according to Skyroot. It also features pneumatic stage separation systems and an onboard mission computer called 'Ramanujan' — named after the legendary mathematician — that processes data from every sensor and makes real-time flight decisions.

The mission's primary objective was to validate the vehicle's propulsion, avionics, telemetry, guidance, navigation, and control systems under actual flight conditions. All major flight events — including stage separations and orbital insertion — were completed successfully.

The Payloads: Science, Art, and a PM's Postcard

"Before these reforms, orbital launches from Indian soil were the exclusive domain of ISRO.</p> <p>"The first-ever Indian private sector launch has been successfully completed."

Vikram-1's maiden flight carried a diverse mix of technology-demonstration payloads and symbolic cargo. On the scientific side, the rocket deployed payloads from Grahaa Space, Cosmoserve Space's Mission Embrace robotic technology, components from German company DCubed, and Skyroot's own in-house SCOPE payload.

But the mission also carried some decidedly unconventional cargo. 'Cosmic Bloom,' a lab-grown diamond artwork by Cosmos Diamonds, went to orbit, along with a micro-art piece featuring 18-karat gold sculptures of three legends of Indian science — Sir C.V. Raman, Dr. Vikram Sarabhai, and Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam — each smaller than a grain of rice.

And in a poignant symbolic gesture, a handwritten postcard by Prime Minister Narendra Modi bearing the words "Vande Mataram" traveled aboard Vikram-1, alongside handwritten messages from Skyroot team members, scientists, policymakers, investors, current and former ISRO chairpersons, and Indian astronauts.

Modi Calls It 'a Defining Moment'

Prime Minister Modi was personally invested in the mission's success. Before launch, he posted on X urging Indians — especially young people — to follow the historic mission, calling it "a historic new frontier for India's space journey."

"This mission highlights the talent, determination and entrepreneurial spirit of India's youth and it shows how Indian space sector reforms are unlocking new opportunities for innovation and enterprise."

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi, ahead of Vikram-1 launch

After the successful orbit insertion, Modi spoke directly to the Skyroot team over the phone, telling them: "This is a defining moment in India's space journey. The growing participation of our private sector is opening new frontiers and accelerating innovation. This achievement will encourage countless youngsters to dream bigger and innovate fearlessly."

The Prime Minister had also recently inaugurated Skyroot's Infinity Campus in Hyderabad via video conference, calling it a symbol of India's rising space ambitions and the strength of its private sector.

From ISRO Labs to a Billion-Dollar Startup

Skyroot's journey from a two-person startup to India's first spacetech unicorn is itself a remarkable story. Founded in 2018 by Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka — both former ISRO engineers — the company set out to build modular, cost-effective launch vehicles for the booming global small-satellite market.

The startup first made history in November 2022 with Vikram-S, India's first privately built suborbital rocket. That mission served as a technology demonstrator, proving that an Indian startup could build and fly a rocket. Vikram-1 was the logical next step — a full orbital-class vehicle.

The path to Saturday's launch was paved with capital. Just two months ago, Skyroot raised $60 million in a round co-led by Sherpalo Ventures — founded by Ram Shriram, one of Google's earliest investors and a board member at Alphabet — and GIC, Singapore's sovereign wealth fund. Funds managed by BlackRock, Playbook Partners, the Shanghvi Family Office, and the founders of Greenko Group also participated. The round valued Skyroot at $1.1 billion pre-money, more than doubling its previous $500 million valuation from 2023 and bringing total funding to $160 million.

Skyroot's Infinity Campus in Hyderabad, spread over 200,000 square feet, has been designed to manufacture one orbital rocket every month — an ambition that moves India closer to competing with established commercial launch providers like Rocket Lab and Firefly Aerospace in the United States.

What Comes Next

Skyroot is not resting on this milestone. Following the successful maiden mission, the company plans up to two more Vikram-1 launches this year to build a flight heritage before opening the vehicle to routine commercial service. In the first quarter of 2027, it intends to introduce Vikram-1U, an upgraded version fitted with strap-on boosters for greater payload capacity.

Simultaneously, Skyroot is developing Vikram-2, a significantly more powerful one-tonne-class launch vehicle powered by a cryogenic upper stage — technology that would put the company in a different league entirely.

"The small satellite launch market is deeply constrained on the supply side," CEO Pawan Kumar Chandana said ahead of the launch. "At the same time, the demand for services enabled by satellites in space will only continue to grow, and that is where Skyroot's opportunity lies."

A Watershed for India's Space Economy

Vikram-1's successful orbit is not just a win for one company. It represents the most significant outcome yet of India's 2020 space sector reforms, which for the first time opened launch activities to private companies under the supervision of IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre). Before these reforms, orbital launches from Indian soil were the exclusive domain of ISRO.

"The first-ever Indian private sector launch has been successfully completed. Not only did it meet the mission objectives, it deployed all the payloads as intended," the IN-SPACe chairperson confirmed.

The timing is significant. India's spacetech sector is projected to become a $77 billion market by 2030, and the government aims to build a $44 billion space economy by 2033. Industrial groups including Larsen & Toubro and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited are also moving into rocket manufacturing, but Skyroot has gotten there first — and with a privately developed vehicle.

"We have done everything that could be done to test Vikram-1 on the ground. On 18 July, we are eager to see how Vikram-1 performs in a real flight environment for the first time."

— Pawan Kumar Chandana, Co-founder and CEO, Skyroot Aerospace

For the Indian diaspora watching from around the world, the launch carries a particular resonance. It is proof that India's engineering talent — much of it trained at institutions like IITs and ISRO — can build globally competitive space technology from scratch, funded by global capital, on Indian soil. The names on the rocket's stages tell the story: Kalam, after the missile man who became president; Raman, after the Nobel laureate; Ramanujan, after the self-taught mathematical genius. Vikram itself honors Dr. Vikram Sarabhai, the father of India's space program.

On a July afternoon in Sriharikota, all of that heritage took flight.
